_comment: The report's cumulative section, one entry per aggregate. Each entry names the tree it describes, so a figure that has fallen behind the branch says so in the rendered table instead of relying on someone remembering. `file` is a perf/scripts/compare_screen.py output under perf/baselines/; `figures` is for an aggregate that is not screen output.
_stock_comment: The commit the stock arm of every aggregate here was measured against. verify_report.py asserts the ref still resolves to it: if next moves, the figures describe a tree that no longer exists and want re-measuring, which should fail a check rather than be noticed by someone eventually.

aggregates.label: Read loop, 57 scenarios
aggregates.note:
median of five alternating rounds per arm, both arms proved distinct by content hash -- stock `0ee05ec157bcf7a8`, branch `33f4cb8930f61178` -- and each hash reproduced on every arm of every round. Query counts were bit-identical across all rounds on both arms (3,619 and 901): zero unstable counts in any run.

**Wall clock is the median of each scenario across the five rounds, then summed** -- not the median of the five round totals. Summing rounds first lets the single largest endpoint drive the result, and `api.interface.depth1` at ~11s is large enough to do it.

Dispersion across rounds is **0.74% on stock and 0.95% on branch**, as the interquartile range of the round totals against their median. Max-min is wider, 3.96% and 1.56%, but it grows with round count by construction and is not comparable with the three-round figures this row used to carry. **Per scenario the picture is looser: the median scenario's relative standard deviation across rounds is 5.21% on stock and 5.25% on branch.** The totals are stable because 57 scenarios' errors cancel, not because any single endpoint reproduces tightly -- so this cumulative figure carries weight that an individual per-endpoint wall-clock number taken from it does not.

**Re-measured 2026-09-22, after the branch was rebased onto `next` at 3f77053a7.** The stock arm moved with it, so both arms now carry the 22 queries finding 88 attributes to upstream #9501 -- which is why the query row reads -75.1% where it read -75.6%, the branch's absolute saving being unchanged at 2,718 queries. The scenario set is hand-picked and largely what this branch optimised, so it describes these pages fairly rather than predicting an arbitrary one; the read screen row is the unbiased check

aggregates.label: Read screen, every REST read endpoint
aggregates.note:
median of three alternating rounds per arm with the arm ORDER reversed between rounds, enumerated from the URL resolver at run time rather than from a scenario list, and matched on `(id, kind)` -- the kinds make 518 measurements, and keying on id alone collapses them to 165 and silently changes every total. Arms proved distinct by content hash on every swap.

**Direction, not just the net: 51 measurements improved, 332 unchanged, 133 worse.** The 133 are finding 62's trade made visible -- a prefetch replacing a JOIN is more round trips, each cheaper -- and that finding's own note says the query counter reads it as a regression and must not be the gate. They cost 248 queries against 10,615 saved, 2.3%, and the same rounds put database time down 41.4%.

This row exists to check whether the read loop's result generalises beyond the 57 scenarios this branch optimised. It is REST-only -- no UI page appears in it -- and it is a screening instrument read as a ranked list, not a gate

aggregates.label: Write screen, every POST endpoint
aggregates.note:
median of three alternating rounds per arm, matched on `(id, kind)` rather than id alone -- the three kinds make 257 measurements from 105 endpoints, and keying on id alone collapses them. Arms proved distinct by content hash on every swap.

178 measurements improved, 66 unchanged, 10 worse. **Queries and wall clock come apart on the write path and both belong here**: -17.0% queries against -30.7% wall. Gating on queries alone undervalues the write-path work by roughly 1.8x, because those wins are Python -- serializer reuse, natural-key memoization, a tag cache -- rather than SQL

aggregates.coverage: 11,572 objects created per arm, across 68 models
aggregates.label: Whole-workflow apply, 11,572 objects
aggregates.note:
**the whole-workflow figure: one `databot apply` per arm, creating 11,572 objects across 68 models, three alternating rounds, median.** The database is dropped and recreated from an empty template before every arm, so each run builds the dataset from nothing.

The client runs on a second host, not on the box under measurement: it builds every payload itself and is a sustained CPU load, and the perf overlay commits all eight of the measurement host's threads. Measured cost of moving it off-box is +0.16ms per TCP connect against ~198ms average per request.

Wall clock is tight across rounds -- stock 1839/1838/1832s, branch 1037/1040/1032s, spans of 0.4% and 0.8% -- and row counts were identical on all six arms (536 devices, 1,616 interfaces, 1,648 cables), which is what says each arm applied the same work. Query counts come from `pg_stat_statements` reset per arm, so they cover the whole run rather than one request.

The dataset file defines 11,578 objects and databot reports creating 11,572; the six-object difference was not chased, and the figures here describe what was created. The figures are computed from the run's own result lines by `perf/scripts/compare_apply.py`, so verify_report.py recomputes this row like any other. It was hand-entered until 2026-09-23
